title: What a stable sort guarantees
question: Which property defines a stable sorting algorithm?
options: Records with equal keys keep the same relative order they had in the input
The algorithm never needs more than a constant amount of extra memory while it runs on any input
The running time stays at O(n log n) no matter how the input values happen to be arranged
The algorithm performs exactly the same number of comparisons for every input of size n
explanation: Stability only concerns equal keys: if two records compare equal, the one that came first in the input still comes first in the output. That is what makes multi-key sorting by successive passes work. Constant extra memory describes in-place sorting, and a fixed running time or comparison count are separate properties that say nothing about the order of ties.

title: Insertion sort on sorted input
question: Roughly how many steps does insertion sort need when the input is already sorted?
options: About n log n steps, because each element is still located by halving the sorted prefix first
About n squared steps, because every pair of elements is always compared at least once
About log n steps, because the algorithm detects early that nothing at all has to be moved
About n steps, because each element is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put
explanation: Insertion sort shifts an element left only while the element before it is larger. On sorted input that test fails immediately, so each of the n elements costs one comparison and the total is linear. The n squared cost appears for reversed input, the usual implementation does not halve anything, and it still has to look at every element, so it cannot finish in logarithmic time.

title: Merge sort time and space
question: Which statement about merge sort is correct for an array of n elements?
options: It runs in O(n log n) time on average but degrades to O(n squared) time on already sorted data
It runs in O(n squared) time in every case but sorts the array fully in place without a buffer
It runs in O(n log n) time in every case but typically needs O(n) extra space for merging
It runs in O(n) time because each element is merged into the final result exactly one time
explanation: Merge sort splits the array about log n times and each level merges n elements, giving O(n log n) regardless of input order; the merge step needs an auxiliary buffer proportional to n. The quadratic worst case on sorted data is a trait of naive quicksort, not of merge sort. Each element is merged at every one of the log n levels, so the total is not linear.

title: Limit of comparison sorting
question: What is the best worst-case cost any algorithm can achieve when it sorts only by comparing pairs of elements?
options: Omega(n) comparisons are enough, because every element only has to be read one time
Omega(n log n) comparisons are unavoidable in the worst case for n elements
Omega(log n) comparisons are enough, because each comparison halves the remaining work
Omega(n squared) comparisons are unavoidable, because every pair has to be checked once
explanation: A comparison sort must distinguish among n! possible orderings, and each comparison has only two outcomes, so it needs at least log2(n!) comparisons, which is on the order of n log n. Reading each element once or halving work cannot separate all orderings, and checking every pair is wasteful because merge sort and heapsort beat n squared. Counting sort escapes the bound only by not comparing keys.

title: Meaning of in-place sorting
question: What does it mean when a sorting algorithm is described as in-place?
options: It never moves an element farther than one single position away from where it started
It rearranges the elements inside the input array using only O(1) additional memory
It keeps a second sorted copy of the data so that the original array stays untouched
It sorts the data directly on disk instead of loading the whole input into main memory
explanation: In-place means the algorithm reorders the original array and uses only a small, constant amount of extra storage, as insertion sort and heapsort do. Limiting movement to one position is not required, and heapsort in fact moves elements far. Keeping a sorted copy is the opposite of in-place, and sorting on disk is called external sorting.

title: Binary search precondition
question: What must be true about the data before binary search can be applied to it?
options: The elements must be ordered and allow direct access to the middle position
The elements must be distinct and stored without any gaps between neighbouring items
The elements must be integers that fit inside a fixed and known numeric range of values
The elements must have been inserted in the same order in which they will be searched
explanation: Binary search discards half of the range by comparing the target with the middle element, which only works if the data is ordered, and it needs cheap access to the middle. Duplicates are allowed, the values do not have to be integers (any comparable type works), and insertion order matters only because it may leave the data unsorted.

title: When binary search gives up
question: In a binary search over indexes lo..hi, what tells you the target is not in the array?
options: The middle element is larger than the target on the very first comparison that is made
The value of lo and the value of hi become exactly equal to each other at some step
The middle index lands on the first or on the last position of the array during the search
The search range becomes empty because lo has moved past hi
explanation: Each step keeps only the half that could still hold the target, so when no indexes remain (lo greater than hi) every candidate has been ruled out. Equal lo and hi leaves one candidate that still must be tested. A single comparison with a larger middle only discards the right half, and landing on an end position proves nothing.

title: Binary search on a linked list
question: Why is binary search a poor fit for a sorted singly linked list?
options: A linked list cannot hold sorted data, because its nodes are scattered around in memory
Binary search only works on structures whose length is known before the search starts
Reaching the middle node requires walking the list, so the logarithmic advantage is lost
Linked lists store their keys as pointers, which cannot be compared with a less-than test
explanation: Binary search relies on jumping to the middle element in constant time. A linked list has no index, so each probe means walking node by node, which costs O(n) overall and makes a plain linear scan just as good. A linked list can be kept sorted, its length can be tracked, and node keys are ordinary comparable values.

title: Duplicates in binary search
question: An array holds the value 7 several times. What does a basic binary search for 7 return?
options: Always the lowest index holding 7, because the search starts from the left side of the array
Always the highest index holding 7, because the range keeps shrinking toward the right side
Any index holding 7, with no promise that it is the first or the last one
No index at all, because binary search cannot handle repeated values stored in an array
explanation: The basic algorithm stops as soon as the middle element equals the target, and which copy it lands on depends on the array size and layout. Finding the first or last occurrence needs a variant that keeps searching after a match. The search does not start from either end, and duplicates do not break it.

title: Space used by binary search
question: How much extra memory does an iterative binary search need beyond the input array?
options: O(log n), since it stores one index for every halving step that it performs
O(1), since it only tracks a few index variables such as lo, hi and mid
O(n), since it keeps a copy of the half that is still being searched at each step
O(n log n), since it records every comparison that it makes while narrowing the range
explanation: The iterative version just updates lo, hi and mid, so memory stays constant. A recursive version uses O(log n) stack frames, which is where the logarithmic figure comes from, but the iterative one does not. Neither version copies the remaining half or records its comparisons.

title: What two pointers means
question: What is the core idea of the two-pointers technique on an array?
options: Two indexes move through the data, often toward each other, so one pass replaces a nested loop
Two copies of the array are sorted separately and then merged back together into a single array
Two threads scan the array at the same time and share a lock around every comparison they do
Two hash tables record every value seen so far so that duplicates can be skipped quickly
explanation: The technique keeps two indexes (for example one at each end, or a slow and a fast one) and moves them according to a rule, which often cuts an O(n squared) pair search down to O(n). It has nothing to do with copying and merging arrays, with multithreading, or with maintaining hash tables.

title: Palindrome check with two pointers
question: How does a two-pointers palindrome check on a string work?
options: One index scans forward while a second index jumps ahead by two characters at each step
Both indexes start at the first character and the second one runs ahead until it finds a mismatch
One index walks the string once and the other counts how many characters were repeated
One index starts at each end, they compare characters and move toward the middle
explanation: A palindrome reads the same in both directions, so the first and last characters must match, then the second and second-to-last, and so on. Two indexes converging from the ends do that in O(n) time and O(1) space. The other schemes do not pair mirrored positions, so they cannot verify the property.

title: Why sorting helps two pointers
question: Why does the opposite-ends two-pointers method for finding a pair with a given sum require sorted input?
options: Order makes every pair add up to the same total, so the pointers are able to stop at once
Order guarantees that the array holds no duplicates, which would otherwise break the pointers
Order lets both pointers move in the same direction without ever crossing each other at all
Order tells you which pointer to move: a sum too small needs a larger left value
explanation: With sorted data, a sum below the target can only be raised by advancing the left pointer, and a sum above it can only be lowered by retreating the right one, so each step safely discards a candidate. Sorting does not equalise pair sums, remove duplicates or make the pointers travel the same way.

title: Finding the middle node
question: How can fast and slow pointers find the middle of a singly linked list in one pass?
options: Advance both pointers by one node each step, and the node where they meet is the middle
Advance slow by two nodes and fast by one, and the node where they swap is the middle
Advance slow by one node and fast by two, and slow sits at the middle when fast ends
Advance fast to the end first, then count the nodes so that slow can step back halfway
explanation: Since fast covers twice the distance of slow, when fast reaches the end slow has covered half the list. Pointers moving at the same speed never separate, the speeds in the third scheme are reversed, and counting then stepping back is impossible in a singly linked list and would need extra passes.

title: Read and write pointers
question: What roles do the two indexes play when removing a given value from an array in place with two pointers?
options: A left index collects the removed values while a right index collects all of the kept values
A read index visits every element and a write index marks where the next kept value goes
A first index remembers the original array while a second index builds a sorted copy of it
A fast index finds the removed value and a slow index deletes it by shifting everything after it
explanation: The read pointer scans each element once; whenever the element is one to keep, it is copied to the write pointer's position, which then advances. The result is O(n) time and O(1) extra space with no repeated shifting. The other descriptions either need extra storage or shift elements repeatedly.

title: What a sliding window is
question: What does the sliding window technique maintain while it scans an array?
options: A contiguous range of elements whose boundaries move forward as the scan advances
A set of non-adjacent elements chosen so as to maximise a value over the whole array
A sorted copy of the data that is updated every single time a new element is read
A stack of previously visited positions that can be revisited later in reverse order
explanation: The window is a contiguous subarray or substring delimited by a left and a right boundary; as the right side grows and the left side advances, the window slides along the data while reusing work from the previous position. It is about adjacent elements, not arbitrary subsets, sorted copies or stacks.

title: Updating a fixed-size window
question: A window of fixed size k moves one step to the right. How is its running sum updated cheaply?
options: Add the element that enters and subtract the element that leaves the window
Recompute the sum of all k elements from scratch so that no stale value can remain in it
Add the element that enters and divide the whole sum by the window size k each time
Subtract the first element of the entire array and add the last element of the entire array
explanation: Only two elements differ between consecutive windows, so adding the entering one and subtracting the leaving one costs O(1) instead of O(k). Recomputing from scratch is the slow approach the technique avoids, dividing by k turns the sum into an average, and the ends of the whole array are irrelevant to the window.

title: Why a window scan is linear
question: Why does a variable-size sliding window over n elements run in O(n) time even though it has a loop inside a loop?
options: The inner loop is skipped for most elements because the window is usually found to be empty
The inner loop always runs exactly twice, regardless of the size of the array being scanned
The window shrinks to half of its size after every step, which gives a logarithmic cost
Each boundary only moves forward, so every element enters and leaves the window once
explanation: The left and right boundaries never move backwards, so together they make at most 2n moves across the entire scan, which amortises to O(n). The inner loop is not skipped or fixed at two iterations, and the window does not halve; its size depends on the data.

title: When sliding window applies
question: Which kind of question is a natural fit for a sliding window?
options: Finding the best subset of items whose total weight stays under a given limit
Finding the shortest route between two nodes in a graph that has weighted edges
Finding the longest contiguous substring whose characters satisfy a condition
Finding whether a value exists anywhere in a collection that has no particular order
explanation: A sliding window works when the answer is a contiguous block, so extending or shrinking the block by one element only changes a little state. Choosing arbitrary subsets is a knapsack-style problem, shortest routes call for graph algorithms, and unordered membership tests are served by a scan or a hash lookup.

title: Shrinking a variable window
question: In a variable-size window, what do you do when the window stops satisfying its constraint after the right side grows?
options: Reset both boundaries to the start of the array and begin the whole scan over again
Advance the left boundary, removing elements, until the constraint holds again
Stop the whole scan immediately, since no later window can ever satisfy the constraint
Advance the right boundary even further so that more elements can repair the constraint
explanation: Moving the left boundary drops elements from the window and restores validity, and the scan then continues; this is what keeps the process linear. Resetting to the start would repeat work, stopping early would miss valid later windows, and growing further only adds more elements to an already invalid window.

title: Reading matrix dimensions
question: A matrix has 4 rows and 6 columns. How many elements does it hold, and how is its size usually written?
options: 10 elements, written 4 x 6 with the row count first
24 elements, written 4 x 6 with the row count first
24 elements, written 6 x 4 with the column count first
10 elements, written 6 x 4 with the column count first
explanation: Size is conventionally written rows x columns, so 4 rows and 6 columns is a 4 x 6 matrix. Every row holds 6 values and there are 4 rows, so there are 4 times 6 = 24 elements; adding the dimensions (10) confuses a sum with a product. Writing columns first is not the standard convention.

title: Matrix product shape
question: Matrix A is 2 x 3 and matrix B is 3 x 5. What happens when you compute A times B?
options: The product is defined and has shape 2 x 5
The product is defined and has shape 3 x 3
The product is defined and has shape 5 x 2
The product is undefined because the shapes are different
explanation: Multiplication needs the number of columns of A to equal the number of rows of B, which holds here (3 and 3). The result takes the rows of A and the columns of B, so it is 2 x 5. The shared dimension disappears, and shapes do not have to be identical for a product to exist.

title: Main diagonal indexes
question: In a square matrix stored as m[row][col], which cells form the main diagonal?
options: The cells where the row index plus the column index equals n minus one
The cells in the first row together with the cells in the last column
The cells where the row index is strictly greater than the column index
The cells where the row index equals the column index
explanation: The main diagonal runs from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner, visiting m[0][0], m[1][1], m[2][2] and so on, so row equals column. Row plus column equal to n minus one describes the anti-diagonal, and a row index greater than the column index describes the cells strictly below the diagonal.

title: Symmetric matrix
question: Which condition makes a square matrix symmetric?
options: Every element on the main diagonal is zero while all of the other elements are different
Every row is an exact copy of the row that comes immediately before it in the matrix
Every element equals its mirror across the main diagonal: m[i][j] equals m[j][i]
Every element equals the negative of its mirror across the main diagonal of the matrix
explanation: A symmetric matrix is unchanged by transposition, which means swapping row and column indexes gives the same value. Zeros on the diagonal are not required, identical rows describe a different structure, and a matrix whose mirror entries are negatives of each other is called skew-symmetric.

title: Cost of visiting every cell
question: How long does it take to visit every cell of a matrix with r rows and c columns exactly once?
options: O(r + c), proportional to the sum of the dimensions
O(log r + log c), because the cells can be split in halves
O(r x c), proportional to the number of cells
O(r x c x c), because each cell also scans its whole row
explanation: Each of the r x c cells is touched one time, so the cost is proportional to the cell count (O(n squared) for a square matrix of side n). The sum of the dimensions would cover only a single row and column, halving does not let you skip cells you must still visit, and rescanning the row would add a needless factor.

title: Prefix sum definition
question: In a prefix-sum array built over a[0..n-1] with prefix[0] = 0, what does prefix[i] hold?
options: The sum of the elements of a from a[i] all the way up to the last element
The sum of the first i elements of a, from a[0] up to a[i - 1]
The sum of only the two elements a[i - 1] and a[i] that sit next to each other
The running product of the first i elements of a, from a[0] up to a[i - 1]
explanation: A prefix sum stores cumulative totals from the start, so prefix[i] accumulates a[0] through a[i - 1] and prefix[0] is the empty sum. The suffix total is a different array, the sum of two neighbours is a pairwise sum, and a running product is a prefix product rather than a prefix sum.

title: Cost of prefix sums
question: What is the cost profile of using prefix sums to answer range-sum queries on a fixed array?
options: O(n) once to build the table, then O(1) for each range query
O(1) to build the table, then O(n) for each range query that follows
O(n log n) to build the table, then O(log n) for each range query that follows
O(n) to build the table, then O(n) again for each range query that follows
explanation: Building the table is one pass over the array, and afterwards any range sum is a single subtraction of two stored values. A scan per query would cost O(n) each, the build cannot be constant because every element must be read, and no sorting or tree is involved, so the logarithmic figures do not apply.

title: Why prefix[0] is zero
question: Why do range-sum implementations usually make the prefix array one slot longer and set prefix[0] to 0?
options: So the array can store the total of all elements in a spot that is easy to find later
So queries on an empty array return a random value rather than raising an error at all
So the build loop can run backwards from the last element toward the first element
So a range that starts at index 0 uses the same subtraction formula as every other range
explanation: With a leading zero, the sum of a[l..r] is always prefix[r + 1] minus prefix[l], even when l is 0, so no special case is needed. The total is available anyway at the final slot, empty-array queries should be deterministic, and the direction of the build loop is unrelated to the sentinel.

title: Prefix sums and updates
question: What is the main drawback of a prefix-sum table when the array values change frequently?
options: Changing one element makes all earlier prefix entries wrong, so the table must be rebuilt
Changing one element is impossible, because prefix tables are always read-only structures
Changing one element only works if the new value is larger than the one it replaces
Changing one element forces every later prefix entry to be corrected, costing O(n)
explanation: Each prefix entry includes all elements before it, so an update at position i alters entries from i onwards, which is O(n) in the worst case. Earlier entries stay valid, tables can be rewritten like any array, and the new value need not be larger. Structures like Fenwick trees handle frequent updates better.

title: When prefix sums pay off
question: For which workload is building a prefix-sum table clearly worthwhile?
options: A single range-sum query on an array that is discarded right after it is answered
A single lookup of one element by index in an array that never changes at all
Many different range-sum queries on an array that does not change between them
A workload in which every query is followed by an update to many of the elements
explanation: The O(n) build is repaid when it is shared by many O(1) queries. With only one query, a direct loop over the range costs no more than building the table, a lookup by index needs no sums at all, and frequent updates keep invalidating the table.
